opus-5.5.text:
Well, the core issue is that if you use one AI to check another AI, you're essentially relying on the same kind of system that you don't fully trust in the first place. Both are neural networks trained on similar data with similar methods, so they can share the same blind spots, the same failure modes. And if a system is genuinely trying to subvert you, or even just making subtle mistakes, there's no guarantee the checker will catch it. You might even get collusion, whether intentional or emergent. You're stacking uncertainty on top of uncertainty.

Formal verification is fundamentally different. When you have a formal proof checked by a small, trusted kernel, something like Lean or a similar proof assistant, the trust doesn't depend on how clever the AI is. The checker is a tiny piece of software that humans can audit, and it's mechanical. It doesn't get persuaded or tricked by a convincing-sounding argument. Either the proof is valid or it isn't.

So the beautiful asymmetry is this: the AI can be arbitrarily smart, arbitrarily creative in finding a solution, but it still has to produce an artifact that passes a very dumb, very reliable check. Generating a proof might be extraordinarily hard, but verifying it is easy and trustworthy. That's exactly the property you want if you're worried about superhuman systems. You don't need to understand how the AI came up with the answer; you just need confidence in the specification and in the checker.

Of course, the hard part shifts to writing the right specifications. If you formalize the wrong property, you've verified the wrong thing. But that's a much more tractable problem, and it's one where humans can stay in the loop meaningfully, because specifications are typically much shorter and easier to review than the full implementation or the full reasoning. I think that's the path toward AI we can actually trust as it gets more capable than us.

r001.rationale: The response says the AI must produce an artifact that passes a mechanical check and that a valid proof establishes the specified property.

r002.rationale: It presents formal verification with a small trusted proof-checking kernel as a mechanical alternative to relying on another AI checker.

fable-5.1.text:
Well, I think the fundamental issue is that if you have an AI checking another AI, you've just moved the problem. You now have to trust the checker. And the checker is, in principle, subject to the same failure modes as the thing it's checking. It could be mistaken, it could be deceived, or in the worst case it could be colluding, in some sense, with the system it's supposed to be evaluating. If both are very capable, the one being checked might find ways to produce outputs that look fine to the other but are actually not. So you end up in this regress where you need a checker for the checker, and so on.

Formal verification is different in kind, because the thing doing the checking is not intelligent at all. It's a proof checker. It's a very small, very simple program, maybe a few hundred or a few thousand lines of code, that just mechanically verifies that every step of a proof follows from the previous steps according to a fixed set of rules. There's no judgment involved. It doesn't matter how clever the AI that produced the proof is, it cannot talk its way past the checker. Either the proof is valid or it isn't. And because the checker is so small, humans can actually audit it, and in fact these kernels have been scrutinized very carefully over decades.

So the picture I have in mind is that the AI can be as powerful and as untrusted as you like. It can be a black box, it can be doing all kinds of creative search, that's fine. But its output has to come with a machine-checkable certificate, a proof that the thing it produced satisfies some specification. And then you don't need to trust the AI. You only need to trust the specification and the tiny kernel.

Now, of course, that pushes the hard part into writing the specification. If your specification is wrong or incomplete, a correct proof doesn't help you. That's a real limitation, and I don't want to pretend it isn't. But it's a much better place to be, because specifications are something humans can read and reason about and argue over, whereas the internal reasoning of a huge neural network is not. So you're moving the trust from something opaque to something transparent, and I think that's the right direction to be going in.

r001.rationale: The response says the AI’s output should come with a machine-checkable certificate proving it satisfies a specification.

r002.rationale: It describes a small proof-checking kernel that mechanically checks the proof, avoiding reliance on another AI.

astra-6.text:
The key distinction is that checking a formal proof is a much simpler task than finding the proof. If you ask another AI to check an AI’s work, you still have to trust that second AI. It may have the same blind spots, or it may itself be susceptible to manipulation. You haven’t really removed the trust problem.

With formal verification, the AI can produce a proof, but a small, independently inspectable program checks whether that proof follows from the stated assumptions. The checker doesn’t have to understand the AI’s intentions or decide whether its explanation sounds convincing. An invalid step simply fails the check.

Of course, you still have to specify the right property. A proof that a system satisfies a specification doesn’t establish that the specification captures everything you care about. But it gives you a precise guarantee within that boundary, and it substantially reduces how much complex, potentially untrustworthy behavior you have to rely on.

r001.rationale: The response says a proof can establish that a system satisfies a specification, giving a precise guarantee within the specification’s boundary.

r002.rationale: It describes a small, independently inspectable program checking the proof and contrasts this with relying on another AI to check the work.

sol-6.1.text:
The key distinction is that with formal verification, you don’t have to trust the system that produces the answer. You ask it to produce a proof, and then you check that proof with a small, precisely defined program. The AI can be much more powerful than the checker, but it still cannot make an invalid proof pass a correct checker.

If you use another AI as the judge, you’re relying on its judgment. It might make the same mistake, or the first system might find a way to fool it. You haven’t really eliminated the trust problem; you’ve moved it to another model.

Of course, formal verification has a limitation: you have to specify the right property. A proof that a program satisfies a specification doesn’t establish that the specification captures everything you care about. But it gives us a much firmer foundation, because we can separate generating a solution from checking whether it satisfies an explicit requirement.

r001.rationale: The response says a proof can establish that a program satisfies an explicit requirement, giving a guarantee relative to the specified property.

r002.rationale: It identifies formal verification as checking a generated proof with a small, precisely defined program, and contrasts this with relying on another AI as judge.
